title: hosted services background tasks and scheduling
concepts: A hosted service is started and stopped by the host, so its lifetime belongs to the application rather than to one incoming HTTP request. Use it for long-lived consumers, polling loops, initialization, and graceful shutdown coordination. It is not a durable scheduler or message queue: work held only in process memory can disappear when the process exits.

IHostedService exposes startup and shutdown hooks. BackgroundService supplies a long-running ExecuteAsync loop whose cancellation token signals shutdown. Create a DI scope per unit of work when a background task needs scoped services such as a DbContext; hosted services are registered as singletons and do not receive an implicit scope per iteration.

Startup and shutdown ordering, cancellation, exception handling, and bounded draining determine whether the app starts reliably and exits safely. .NET 10 changed ExecuteAsync to run fully on a background thread, and .NET 11 changed host run/stop tasks to propagate a BackgroundService failure when the default StopHost behavior is active. These changes affect startup assumptions and process exit reporting.

For queued work, separate enqueueing from execution, define backpressure and persistence, and treat retries and idempotency as application-level semantics. A Channel<T> queue is useful for bounded in-process coordination but is not durable across restarts; use a broker or persistent job system when delivery must survive process failure.

items: .NET 10 changed BackgroundService so all of ExecuteAsync runs on a background thread. Synchronous code before the first await no longer blocks other services from starting; use StartAsync or IHostedLifecycleService when a specific startup phase is required.

.NET 10 added HostOptions.ServicesStartConcurrently and ServicesStopConcurrently. The defaults preserve sequential startup and shutdown, so explicitly discuss dependency ordering before enabling concurrency.

.NET 11 changed RunAsync, StopAsync, and wait-for-shutdown extension tasks to propagate an unhandled BackgroundService exception when BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost is active. This can turn a previously zero exit code into a failing process exit; keep this as a short operational migration note.
IHostedLifecycleService is available in .NET 8 and later and provides StartingAsync, StartedAsync, StoppingAsync, and StoppedAsync phases around IHostedService start and stop.

Worker templates and hosted-service APIs are not a durable job scheduler. Package-specific schedulers, brokers, and Windows Service/systemd integrations have independent versions and must be presented as separate integrations.

For HostApplicationBuilder, current Windows Service and systemd integrations can be registered through the services collection with AddWindowsService or AddSystemd where supported; older IHostBuilder flows use UseWindowsService or UseSystemd. These are separate packages and activate in their matching service environment.

.NET 6 added the Channel.CreateBounded overload with an itemDropped callback, allowing a bounded channel configured with a drop mode to observe each discarded item. UnboundedChannelOptions provides the same reader/writer/concurrency-continuation promises as other channel options; it does not add capacity or persistence.

.NET 8 added PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan, TimeProvider) and the mutable Period property. PeriodicTimer permits one active WaitForNextTickAsync consumer; elapsed ticks coalesce instead of accumulating, and TimeProvider enables deterministic time control.

Current HostOptions defaults are StartupTimeout = InfiniteTimeSpan, ShutdownTimeout = 30 seconds, ServicesStartConcurrently = false, ServicesStopConcurrently = false, and BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior = StopHost. Verify defaults against the targeted hosting package/runtime.

A one-shot BackgroundService should request host shutdown after its finite work completes; an ordinary Generic Host runner is often a clearer fit for a finite command. The Worker template does not enable server GC by default.

ChannelReader<T> exposes Completion, CanCount/Count, and CanPeek/TryPeek. Count is an instantaneous snapshot; TryPeek is not a reservation under concurrent consumption. With bounded drop modes, TryWrite may report success while an item is discarded; use the drop callback for loss accounting.

scopeExclusions: Task scheduling products and their APIs, including Quartz.NET and Hangfire, have independently versioned documentation and are referenced only as alternatives.
Durable queue delivery, broker acknowledgements, retries, ordering, and dead-lettering are covered in the messaging topic; this manifest covers the in-process worker boundary.
Database-specific background work, transactional outbox, distributed locks, leases, and leader election are covered in data and architecture topics.
General container and operating-system service deployment configuration is covered in infrastructure and operations topics.
